--- title: "[Poisson]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Poisson family with log (canonical) link. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/main/whittaker/families/poisson.py#L13-L264){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python Poisson() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The Poisson family models the response as non-negative integer counts, such as the number of events observed in a fixed interval of time, space, or exposure. It is the standard choice for count data when the variance of the counts is approximately equal to their mean. The canonical log link guarantees positive fitted values on the response scale and gives the linear predictor a multiplicative interpretation: a one-unit increase in a covariate multiplies the expected count by `exp(coefficient)`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [None]{.doc-parameter-name} : `Poisson` takes no constructor arguments. The scale parameter is fixed at `1` (see `scale_known`), since the Poisson distribution has no free dispersion parameter. ::: ## Notes {.doc-notes} The canonical link is the natural logarithm: $$ g(\mu) = \log(\mu) $$ The variance function is $V(\mu) = \mu$, so the variance equals the mean. If the observed variance substantially exceeds the mean (overdispersion), consider `NegativeBinomial` or `Tweedie` instead. The deviance is $$ D(y, \hat\mu) = 2 \sum_i \left[ y_i \log\!\left(\frac{y_i}{\hat\mu_i}\right) - (y_i - \hat\mu_i) \right] . $$ ## Examples {.doc-examples} Fit a GAM to simulated count data with a smooth, log-linear trend: ::: {#aa77e2b5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import whittaker as wk rng = np.random.default_rng(0) n = 200 x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n) mu = np.exp(0.5 * np.sin(x)) y = rng.poisson(mu) data = {"x": x, "y": y} model = wk.GAM("y ~ s(x)", family=wk.Poisson()) model.fit(data, method="REML") print(model.summary()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` GAM fit summary ============================================================ Formula: y ~ s(x) Family: Poisson(link='log') Observations: 200 Coefficients: 10 Parametric coefficients: Term Estimate Std.Err z value p-value ------------------------ ---------- ---------- ---------- ---------- (Intercept) 0.2113 0.0657 3.214 0.00131 Approximate significance of smooth terms: Term EDF Ref.df Chi.sq p-value ------------------------ ------ ------ ---------- ---------- s(x) 4.18 5 37.260 5.312e-07 Total EDF: 5.18 Deviance: 187.0851 Null dev: 230.5815 Dev. expl: 18.9% GCV score: 0.985797 Scale est: 1.000000 AIC: 554.30 BIC: 571.37 ``` ::: ::: ## Attributes {.doc-attributes}
Name Description
scale_known Whether the dispersion parameter is fixed. Always `True` for Poisson.
### [scale_known]{.doc-object-name .doc-attribute .doc-label .doc-label-property} ::: {.doc-subject} Whether the dispersion parameter is fixed. Always `True` for Poisson. ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-attribute} [scale_known]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} ::: ::: {.doc-text} The Poisson distribution has no free dispersion parameter, so the scale is fixed at `1` and is never estimated during fitting. This affects how `GAM.summary()` reports the scale and how many degrees of freedom are attributed to dispersion estimation. ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
deviance() Total Poisson deviance, the (weighted) sum of `unit_deviance`.
initialize() Starting values for `mu`: `y` nudged away from zero.
link() Apply the log link: $\eta = \log(\mu)$.
link_derivative() Derivative of the log link: $g'(\mu) = 1/\mu$.
link_inverse() Apply the inverse log link: $\mu = e^{\eta}$.
log_likelihood() Poisson log-likelihood $\ell_i = y_i \log(\mu_i) - \mu_i - \log(y_i!)$.
simulate() Simulate Poisson-distributed response values with mean `mu`.
unit_deviance() Per-observation Poisson deviance contributions.
variance() Poisson variance function: $V(\mu) = \mu$.

[mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. [rng]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [np.random.Generator]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A `numpy.random.Generator` instance. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Simulated response values, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [unit_deviance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Per-observation Poisson deviance contributions. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/main/whittaker/families/poisson.py#L157-L182){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python unit_deviance(y, mu) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Computes $d_i = 2 \left[ y_i \log(y_i / \hat\mu_i) - (y_i - \hat\mu_i) \right]$, with the convention $y_i \log(y_i / \hat\mu_i) = 0$ when $y_i = 0$. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [y]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Observed response values (counts), shape `(n,)`. [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Fitted conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Per-observation deviance contributions, shape `(n,)`. ::: ### [variance()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Poisson variance function: $V(\mu) = \mu$. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/whittaker/blob/main/whittaker/families/poisson.py#L117-L133){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python variance(mu) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The variance equals the mean, so `Var(Y) = phi * V(mu) = mu` since `phi = 1` for Poisson (see `scale_known`). ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [mu]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Conditional mean values, shape `(n,)`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [NDArray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Variance values $V(\mu) = \mu$, shape `(n,)`. :::
